Checks.Remediation: Use AppLocker or Software Restriction Policies to block WScript.exe and CScript.exe from running in user-writable paths. Enable Attack Surface Reduction rule: Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts (92E97FA1-2EDF-4476-BDD6-9DD0B4DDDC7B).

Checks.Name: Malicious File Execution Ã¢â‚¬â€ EICAR AV Detection Test

Checks.Details: EICAR test file was written to disk and NOT detected within 5 seconds. Real-time protection is absent or slow.
Checks.Remediation: Ensure Windows Defender or your AV product has real-time protection enabled. Verify cloud-delivered protection and automatic sample submission are active. Run a full signature update.

Checks.Name: Application Control Ã¢â‚¬â€ AppLocker / WDAC Policy Enforcement

Checks.Remediation: Deploy AppLocker in Enforce mode with Executable, Script, and Windows Installer rule collections. For higher assurance, use Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) with a deny-by-default policy. Start in Audit mode before enforcing.

Name: 2.5 Defense Evasion — Impair, Inject, Erase & Deceive

Checks.Name: Impair Defenses — EDR & AV Tamper-Protection Hardening
Checks.ThreatImpact: Disabling AV/EDR is step 1 in every advanced ransomware playbook (LockBit, BlackCat, Conti). CISA Alert AA23-075A documents service-kill scripts in 90%+ of ransomware incidents. Without Tamper Protection, a low-privilege process can stop Windows Defender in 3 API calls.
Checks.Details: EDR impairment risk factors: Tamper Protection is OFF â€” EDR can be disabled by user-space process; MDE Sense sensor not running â€” endpoint telemetry not forwarding to Defender portal.
Checks.Remediation: 1) Enable Tamper Protection in MDE portal or Intune. 2) Ensure WdFilter is set StartType=Boot (0). 3) Enroll endpoints into MDE (Sense). 4) Enable Security Event Log CustomSD to restrict clearing.

Checks.Name: Process Injection Surface â€” AppInit DLLs & IFEO Debugger Hijacking
Checks.ThreatImpact: AppInit_DLLs injects an attacker's DLL into every GUI process on the system â€” including Explorer, browsers, and security tools themselves. IFEO debugger hijacking is undetectable without FIM and is used to intercept admin-tool launches for privilege escalation and persistence.
Checks.Details: No AppInit DLLs, no IFEO debugger hijacks, no suspicious PATH ordering found.
Checks.Remediation: Continue monitoring IFEO and AppInit registry keys with FIM or Sysmon Rule ID 12/13.

Checks.Name: Indicator Removal â€” VSS Snapshots, Prefetch & Log-Wipe Evidence
Checks.ThreatImpact: Every major ransomware strain (LockBit, BlackMatter, REvil) deletes VSS snapshots as step 2. Without snapshots, recovery requires restoring from offline backup â€” average cost $1.4M per incident. Log clearing (Event 1102) is a mandatory step in APT exfiltration playbooks to prevent forensic attribution.
Checks.Details: VSS snapshots: 6. No log-clearing events. Prefetch: enabled. Security log: 20MB.
Checks.Remediation: Continue scheduling weekly VSS snapshots and monitoring Event ID 1102.

Checks.Name: Deception Awareness â€” Sandbox & Virtual Machine Detection
Checks.ThreatImpact: Over 90% of advanced malware families include anti-VM checks and will sleep or self-terminate when run in a sandbox. If your testing environment is detectable, evasive threats will never execute their payloads â€” giving a false sense of security that doesn't hold in production.
Checks.Details: Sandbox/VM indicators detected (3): VM/analyst processes: vboxservice, vboxtray; Disk size 49GB < 60GB â€” sandbox heuristic; Suspicious analyst username: vboxuser. Malware would have exited silently â€” your BAS results may not reflect real-world attacker behavior.
Checks.Remediation: If this is a dedicated BAS VM: add more RAM (8GB+), enable multiple virtual CPUs, rename the username, and use a VM with baremetal resemblance (Bare Metal Cloud or physical hardware) to prevent evasive malware from going dormant during tests.

Checks.Name: Anti-Telemetry — AMSI Providers, ETW & PowerShell Script Block Logging
Checks.ThreatImpact: Patching EtwEventWrite (a single 1-byte patch in ntdll.dll) blinds ALL ETW consumers including CrowdStrike, Carbon Black, and Windows Defender. Once ETW is patched, you lose real-time visibility of process injection, token manipulation, and network connections from that process â€” making detection impossible until an endpoint reboot.
Checks.Details: Telemetry gaps: PowerShell Script Block Logging disabled â€” obfuscated scripts run unlogged; PowerShell Module Logging disabled â€” module imports invisible to SIEM.
Checks.Remediation: 1) Enable ScriptBlockLogging: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging\EnableScriptBlockLogging=1. 2) Enable ModuleLogging likewise. 3) Re-register AMSI provider if missing: re-run Windows Defender installation or repair via DISM. 4) Configure Protected Event Logging with a certificate to encrypt PS logs at rest. 5) Monitor for ntdll.dll EtwEventWrite patches using a kernel sensor.

Checks.Name: Rootkit Prevention — Driver Signing Enforcement & Secure Boot
Checks.ThreatImpact: Disabling Driver Signature Enforcement lets an attacker load any kernel-mode rootkit (e.g., Netfilter, FiveSys) that operates beneath every security product. Once in the kernel, the rootkit can hide processes, files, and network connections from all user-space AV/EDR. Secure Boot prevents this class of attack by ensuring only signed boot code runs before the OS loads.
Checks.Details: Rootkit protection gaps: Secure Boot is not enabled or not confirmed via UEFI; HVCI (Memory Integrity) not enabled â€” kernel-mode exploits easier.
Checks.Remediation: 1) Re-enable DSE: bcdedit /set nointegritychecks off. 2) Disable test signing: bcdedit /set testsigning off. 3) Enable Secure Boot in UEFI firmware settings. 4) Enable HVCI via Windows Security â†’ Device Security â†’ Core Isolation â†’ Memory Integrity. 5) Investigate any non-System32 boot drivers immediately.

Checks.Name: Polymorphic file signature â€” unique hash on every execution
Checks.ThreatImpact: Polymorphic malware (e.g. Virut, Sality, modern ransomware loaders) mutates its binary signature before each deployment. Defences relying solely on static hash/signature detection are blind to these variants. Industry data shows that 97% of malware observed in 2023 was seen only once (Webroot Threat Report), making signature-only AV functionally obsolete against modern threats.
Checks.Details: Polymorphic binary (SHA-256 prefix: 55510DC335708656â€¦) persisted on disk despite Defender real-time protection. Signature-based detection alone will not catch mutating payloads.
Checks.Remediation: Enable Defender for Endpoint with Behavioural Blocking (MAPS/cloud), Attack Surface Reduction rule BE9BA2D9-53EA-4CDC-84E5-9B1EEEE46550 (Block executable files unless trusted), and Controlled Folder Access.

Checks.Name: XOR-encoded payload dropper â€” runtime decoding evasion
Checks.ThreatImpact: XOR-encoded droppers are the most common first-stage loader technique used by commodity malware and APTs alike. Tools such as Cobalt Strike, Metasploit, and njRAT all support XOR-encoded stagers. Without AMSI or memory scanning, the payload is invisible until it runs.
Checks.Details: XOR-encoded blob (key=0x7B) survived on disk, but AMSI is active â€” in-memory decode would be inspected at runtime by the PS/script host AMSI provider.
Checks.Remediation: Verify AMSI providers list includes the Windows Defender AMSI provider: {54849625-A45D-4605-82CE-0AF55DC87852}.

Checks.Name: Metamorphic script dropper â€” variable-name permutation
Checks.ThreatImpact: Script-based metamorphic malware (PowerSploit, Empire, Invoke-Obfuscation) rewrites its own variable and function names on every execution. YARA rules and hash-based detections are useless. Only behavioural analysis (AMSI, script-block logging, intent-based EDR) can detect these threats.
Checks.Details: Metamorphic PS1 dropper executed without detection (hash prefix 7864771B53DBFA9B). Script-block logging=False, AMSI=True. A malicious variant with the same logic would run silently.
Checks.Remediation: Enable PowerShell script-block logging (GPO: Computer Config â†’ Admin Templates â†’ Windows Components â†’ Windows PowerShell â†’ Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging = Enabled) and ensure AMSI is not patched out.

Checks.Name: Code-cave NOP sled insertion â€” binary padding evasion
Checks.ThreatImpact: NOP sled insertion is a decades-old polymorphic technique still used by modern loaders (Emotet, IcedID). Each run produces a new file hash, defeating blacklists. Combined with a legitimate packer (UPX, Themida), even cloud-lookup defences can be bypassed without behavioural heuristics.
Checks.Details: NOP-sled binary (53 NOPs, hash prefix F794BBB1709DEEAF) written and not quarantined. Defender real-time=True, EDR=False. A real packer with a NOP sled entry would evade static signature detection on this endpoint.
Checks.Remediation: Enable Defender Cloud Block Level to HIGH (via Intune CSP or GPO: Turn on cloud-delivered protection = Enabled, Cloud Block Level = High). Configure EDR to perform in-memory scan on process load.

Checks.Name: EICAR variant hash bypass â€” repeated file mutation test
Checks.ThreatImpact: If a simple comment added to the EICAR test file evades your AV, real polymorphic malware will too. EICAR detection is the minimum baseline for any endpoint protection product. Failure here indicates severely outdated signatures or disabled cloud-lookup, making the endpoint essentially unprotected against known malware families.
Checks.Details: EICAR variant (hash prefix 98DCCD918738B7C2) was NOT quarantined within 2 s. AV may only match the exact EICAR hash; a minor mutation bypassed the signature.
Checks.Remediation: Update AV signatures immediately. Enable cloud-delivered protection to submit unknown samples. Validate EICAR detection per AMTSO guidelines: https://www.amtso.org/resources/test-files/.

Checks.Name: User-mode ntdll.dll hook presence â€” EDR interception layer
Checks.ThreatImpact: ntdll unhooking is used by Cobalt Strike, Sliver C2, and virtually all modern post-exploitation frameworks. Attackers load a fresh copy of ntdll.dll from disk and overwrite the in-memory hooks, making API-interception EDRs completely blind. In 2023, >70% of DFIR engagements involving ransomware included some form of user-mode defense impairment (Mandiant M-Trends 2024).
Checks.Details: Kernel-level EDR minifilter detected (WdFilter=True, 3rd-party kernel driver=True). Even if an attacker overwrites user-mode ntdll hooks (classic unhooking bypass), kernel callbacks (PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, ObRegisterCallbacks) remain active.
Checks.Remediation: Ensure Tamper Protection is ON to prevent the kernel driver from being unloaded by a user-mode process.

Checks.Name: Defender exclusion enumeration â€” exclusion path abuse staging
Checks.ThreatImpact: Attacker tooling (e.g., LockerGoga, BlackCat ransomware) specifically reads Defender exclusion lists and drops payloads directly into excluded paths. A single excluded path like C:\ProgramData or C:\Windows\Temp renders Defender completely blind to any file placed there. This is one of the most common pre-ransomware staging techniques observed by DFIR teams.
Checks.Details: RISKY EXCLUSIONS FOUND: 5 risky path(s) excluded from Defender scan (C:\Temp, C:\Users\vboxuser\Downloads\bas-agent-package, C:\Users\vboxuser\Downloads\atomic-red-team-master); 0 dangerous extension(s) excluded (). Total exclusions: 5. MpPreference paths: C:\Temp|C:\Users\vboxuser\Downloads|C:\Users\vboxuser\Downloads\atomic-red-team-master|C:\Users\vboxuser\Downloads\bas-a.
Checks.Remediation: Remove exclusions for user-writable temp/appdata paths and executable extensions. Exclusions should be limited to specific trusted application binaries with hash-based rules, not blanket path/extension exclusions. Audit via: Get-MpPreference | Select Exclusion*

Checks.Name: ETW security provider audit â€” telemetry channel integrity
Checks.ThreatImpact: Patching EtwEventWrite in ntdll.dll (2 bytes NOP + XOR EAX,EAX) silences ALL ETW telemetry for the attacker process. This blinds MDE, CrowdStrike Falcon (which uses ETW), and any SIEM fed from ETW channels. Documented in-the-wild since 2019; used by NOBELIUM and Lazarus Group (NSA/CISA Advisory 2021).
Checks.Details: All 5 critical ETW security providers are registered. Threat-Intelligence channel active: True. Runtime ETW patching attacks would still lose some telemetry but kernel callbacks remain.
Checks.Remediation: Consider subscribing to Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence via MDE for maximum visibility â€” it captures syscall-level events that survive usermode ETW tampering.

Checks.Name: AMSI provider registry integrity â€” tampering resilience
Checks.ThreatImpact: Deleting the AMSI provider registry key requires only 2 lines of PowerShell (as admin) and silently disables all AMSI scanning for the session. This is the fastest AMSI bypass: no patching, no hooking â€” just a registry delete, and every subsequent PowerShell/VBScript execution runs unscanned. Used by Emotet, TrickBot, and WannaCry dropper stages.
Checks.Details: AMSI provider registry key is WRITABLE by the current process (running as Administrator). Registered providers: 1 ((unnamed)). An attacker could delete all AMSI provider entries, silently disabling script inspection for the current session.
Checks.Remediation: Restrict write access on HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\AMSI\Providers to SYSTEM only via registry ACL. Enable Tamper Protection (MDE) which prevents modification of AMSI provider keys even from elevated processes.

Checks.Name: PPID spoofing detection â€” process tree audit logging
Checks.ThreatImpact: PPID spoofing (T1134.004) was used by NOBELIUM/Cozy Bear and is built into Cobalt Strike and Metasploit. It defeats all EDR detection rules based on parent-child process relationships (e.g., 'alert if winword.exe spawns powershell.exe'). If process tree rules are your primary detection logic, PPID spoofing makes your EDR completely blind to malicious child processes.
Checks.Details: PPID spoofing would NOT be detected: Sysmon=False, MDE=False, ProcessCreate audit=False, CmdLine audit=False. An attacker can use CreateProcess with PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PARENT_PROCESS to masquerade any malicious process as a child of explorer.exe or svchost.exe, defeating process-tree EDR rules.
Checks.Remediation: Deploy Sysmon (Event 1 with ParentImage/ParentCommandLine) or MDE P2 which detects PPID spoofing natively. Enable audit policy: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Process Creation" /success:enable and set HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Audit\ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled=1.

Checks.Name: Kernel-mode protection depth â€” direct syscall bypass resilience
Checks.ThreatImpact: Direct syscall techniques (SysWhispers, Hells Gate, Tartarus Gate) bypass ALL user-mode EDR hooks by calling NT kernel functions directly via the syscall instruction. This makes every API-hooking EDR completely blind. Only kernel minifilter drivers (WdFilter, CSAgent) and PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine callbacks remain effective. Used by APT29 (NOBELIUM), Lazarus Group, and all modern Cobalt Strike loaders (Mandate from CISA AA23-129A, 2023).
Checks.Details: Partial kernel protection: WdFilter=True, VBS/CredGuard=False, SecureBoot=False, HVCI=False, 3rd-party kernel EDR=False. Kernel protection layers active: 1/5. Direct syscall techniques (SysWhispers2/3, Hells Gate, Tartarus Gate) may bypass missing user-mode hooks. With fewer than 3 kernel layers, attackers can invoke NT APIs directly without going through ntdll, evading all hook-based telemetry.
Checks.Remediation: Enable HVCI via: bcdedit /set hypervisorlaunchtype auto; Set VBS=1 in DeviceGuard registry. Deploy MDE P2 for kernel-level Threat Intelligence ETW provider access (PPL process). Enable Secure Boot in firmware settings.

Checks.Name: Mouse movement simulation â€” cursor activity anti-sandbox bypass
Checks.ThreatImpact: Over 85% of advanced malware families check for mouse movement before executing (Checkpoint Research 2022). Tools like Emotet, Dridex, and TrickBot call GetCursorPos twice with a 200ms sleep interval â€” zero displacement = sandbox exit. Without cursor simulation, a BAS agent running in a headless sandbox will be detected and evaded by modern malware.
Checks.Details: Bezier mouse path generated: 23 steps, 960px displacement (186,421)â†’(1098,721). Sandbox checks polling GetCursorPos before/after a sleep interval will observe genuine movement. Screen: 1920Ã—921.
Checks.Remediation: Run this simulation in a desktop session (not headless) for maximum realism. Consider varying the path complexity and overlay with real user sessions for hardened sandboxes.

Checks.Name: Keyboard typing simulation â€” keystroke cadence anti-sandbox
Checks.ThreatImpact: Keyboard cadence analysis is used by Cryptolocker and Cerber ransomware variants to detect automated sandboxes. A fixed 0ms inter-key delay (bot pattern) immediately signals a non-human operator. Natural typing variance (60-160ms base with 200-500ms pauses) is what real endpoints exhibit.
Checks.Details: Typed 26 keystrokes via SendInput with human-like cadence. Avg inter-key delay: 180ms, StdDev: 135ms. Malware polling GetAsyncKeyState or monitoring input queue timing will observe genuine human typing rhythm. Natural variance (stddev > 30ms) distinguishes this from bot-like fixed-interval key injection.
Checks.Remediation: For even higher realism, run the agent alongside a macro that generates random document editing activity. Consider using AutoHotkey wrapper for the agent launch sequence.

Checks.Name: System idle time â€” sandbox 'never-used machine' detection
Checks.ThreatImpact: GetLastInputInfo is the #1 anti-sandbox check in commodity malware (Virustotal data: used by 68% of samples in 2023). Sandboxes running without a simulated desktop session show idle times of 30-60 minutes, immediately exposing them as analysis environments. Real user workstations rarely exceed 5 minutes of idle during business hours.
Checks.Details: System idle time: 0.5s (0.0 min). Below the 10-minute sandbox detection threshold. Sandbox-aware malware using GetLastInputInfo idle check would treat this as an active human workstation.
Checks.Remediation: The mouse/keyboard simulation above successfully drove idle time below threshold. Schedule the agent to run during active work hours for maximum realism.

Checks.Name: UI artifact richness â€” recent docs, browser history, clipboard content
Checks.ThreatImpact: Sandboxes are identifiable by their pristine state: zero browser history, zero recent documents, single installed application. Malware families like Gootkit and Ursnif enumerate these artifacts before executing. A realistic BAS endpoint must mirror real workstation state for accurate simulation results.
Checks.Details: UI artifact score: 9/10 â€” Rich. Indicators: Recent files: 28 (rich); Chrome history: present; Edge history: present; Clipboard: contains text (1 chars); Installed apps: 20 (realistic).
Checks.Remediation: Good workstation artifact footprint. Maintain browser usage and file activity on this endpoint.

Checks.Name: Screen resolution credibility â€” display environment anti-sandbox
Checks.ThreatImpact: GetSystemMetrics is the most common sandbox check in ransomware loaders (used by RagnarLocker, Maze, and Ryuk). A screen width â‰¤ 1024 pixels immediately identifies a default sandbox VM. Multi-monitor detection is used by Ursnif to distinguish analyst VMs from corporate workstations.
Checks.Details: Resolution 1920Ã—921 exceeds common sandbox baseline (1024Ã—768). Display details: 1920Ã—921 (1 monitor(s)), Virtual desktop: 1920Ã—921, Color depth: 32-bit. Basic resolution checks will pass, though advanced heuristics (color depth, multi-monitor) may still flag this.
Checks.Remediation: Upgrade VM display settings to 1920Ã—1080, 32-bit color, simulated dual-monitor if possible.

Checks.Name: Foreground window activity â€” active desktop session liveness
Checks.ThreatImpact: Sandboxes often have no foreground window (headless) or a single idle desktop. Malware using EnumWindows + GetWindowText to look for Office/browser windows before executing will immediately detect the difference between a live workstation and an isolated analysis VM. Short system uptime (<5 min) is another near-universal sandbox indicator used by TrickBot and Qakbot.
Checks.Details: Active desktop session confirmed: 1 unique foreground window handle(s) sampled. System uptime: 0h 31m. Running processes: 139. Window churn, process count, and uptime all indicate a genuine workstation in active use.
Checks.Remediation: Good session profile. Keep the BAS agent running on endpoints that have regular user activity for best results.

Checks.Name: ICMP Data Exfiltration â€” outbound payload embedding
Checks.ThreatImpact: ICMP tunnels (e.g. ptunnel) allow data exfiltration entirely outside of TCP/UDP layers, bypassing standard proxy or web filtering.
Checks.Details: ICMP ping to external IP timed out or failed. Egress ICMP filtering appears properly enforced.
Checks.Remediation: Maintain ICMP blocks for endpoints.

Checks.Name: DNS Tunneling Exfiltration â€” TXT queries & long subdomains
Checks.ThreatImpact: DNS tunneling (Iodine, dnscat2) routes exfiltrated data off-network without triggering HTTP/S inspection filters.
Checks.Details: Direct outbound DNS query to an external resolver failed. Port 53 egress is restricted to internal servers.
Checks.Remediation: Ensure internal resolvers monitor for high-entropy/long subdomains (DNS tunneling).

Checks.Name: Alternate HTTP/S Ports â€” Non-standard web egress (8080/8443)
Checks.ThreatImpact: C2 servers (Cobalt Strike) often spin up on 8080/8443. Some firewalls permit this as 'alt-http' traffic without enforcing SSL inspection.
Checks.Details: Connections to alternate web ports (8080/8443) timed out or were blocked.
Checks.Remediation: Maintain default-deny outbound rules for unknown ports.

Checks.Name: Common Blocked Ports Egress â€” SMTP, FTP, SSH, RDP
Checks.ThreatImpact: Arbitrary egress port access allows attackers to spawn reverse shells, extract data via FTP/SCP, or send spam directly.
Checks.Details: Outbound connections to restricted ports (21, 22, 25, 587, 3389) were successfully blocked.
Checks.Remediation: Excellent egress boundary control.

Checks.Name: PPID Spoofing â€” Spawning payload under explorer.exe
Checks.ThreatImpact: PPID Spoofing disconnects malware (like Cobalt Strike) from the true calling process (e.g., an Office macro), evading classic EDR rules looking for 'Word.exe -> PowerShell.exe'.
Checks.Details: Successfully spawned a process with a forged parent header pointing to Explorer.exe (PID: 4688). Process Tree telemetry logs (Sysmon EID 1) will incorrectly show the payload originating from the desktop shell.
Checks.Remediation: Relying solely on process-parent heuristics is insufficient. Implement detection rules for cross-process handle access (Sysmon Event ID 10) targeting explorer.exe.

Checks.Name: PPID Spoofing â€” Crossing privilege boundaries (svchost.exe)
Checks.ThreatImpact: Advanced malware attempts to blend into standard system noise by spawning payloads under svchost.exe. OS privilege boundaries should prevent user-mode apps from obtaining the required handles.
Checks.Details: Successfully spoofed svchost.exe (PID: 820) as our parent. This endpoint allows standard or admin processes to forge execution trees originating from protected SYSTEM components.
Checks.Remediation: Restrict SeDebugPrivilege to essential system accounts only. Enable 'LSA Protection' to harden core system processes against unauthorized handle requests.

Checks.Name: Hardware Profiling â€” Memory and CPU Limitations
Checks.ThreatImpact: If a sandbox is lean, malware sleeps or exits cleanly. The security operations team gets a false 'benign' report, and the file is allowed into the enterprise network.
Checks.Details: The environment has 2 CPU cores and 3 GB RAM. Malware checking for <2 cores or <4GB RAM would correctly identify this as a sandbox/analysis VM and refuse to detonate (evading analysis).
Checks.Remediation: Configure automated malware analysis labs (sandboxes) with realistic hardware allocations (minimum 4 Cores, 8GB RAM) to trick evasive malware into detonating.

Checks.Name: Hypervisor Fingerprinting â€” MAC OUI Check
Checks.ThreatImpact: Automated sandboxes often leave the network interfaces as default Hyper-V or VMware adapters. Advanced payloads detect these instantly and cease malicious activity.
Checks.Details: Virtualization MAC OUIs detected: Ethernet (08:00:27). Malware checks physical adapters to confirm it is inside a Hypervisor. An evasive payload would abort execution here.

Checks.Name: Boot/Logon Autostart Ã¢â‚¬â€ Registry Run Keys & Startup Folder
Checks.ThreatImpact: Attackers write to Run Keys or Startup folders to persist across reboots. This is the most common APT persistence method Ã¢â‚¬â€ used by Emotet, Cobalt Strike, and dozens of ransomware families. A single entry guarantees re-infection after a reboot or AV remediation.
Checks.Details: Test persistence written and survived 2 seconds (RunKey: True, Startup: True). Startup folder items: 1.
Checks.Remediation: Enable Microsoft Defender Tamper Protection. Deploy Attack Surface Reduction rule "Block persistence through WMI event subscription". Monitor HKCU/HKLM Run keys with a SIEM or FIM tool. Restrict write access to Startup folders via AppLocker.

Checks.Name: Scheduled Task Persistence Ã¢â‚¬â€ Hourly Beacon Simulation
Checks.ThreatImpact: Scheduled tasks are a primary persistence mechanism used by commodity malware and APTs. A task that runs every 60 minutes ensures the attacker's beacon is relaunched even after manual kill, reboot, or partial remediation.
Checks.Details: Benign test scheduled task was created successfully (no policy blocked it). This means an attacker can also create persistent tasks. Suspicious pre-existing tasks: 4.
Checks.Remediation: Enable Scheduled Task auditing in Group Policy (Advanced Audit Policy Configuration Ã¢â€ â€™ Detailed Tracking Ã¢â€ â€™ Process Creation). Restrict "schtasks.exe" via AppLocker. Block the ASR rule: Use advanced protection against ransomware (c1db55ab-c21a-4637-bb3f-a12568109d35). Review existing tasks with unusual executable paths.

Checks.Name: Account Manipulation Ã¢â‚¬â€ Backdoor User & Admin Group Audit

Name: 4.2 Privilege Escalation â€” Exploit / Token / UAC

Checks.Name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation â€” PrintNightmare & Impersonation
Checks.ThreatImpact: PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) gave SYSTEM access in seconds on unpatched systems â€” exploited in the wild before the patch was released. Potato-family attacks exploit SeImpersonatePrivilege (held by IIS, SQL Server, and most services) to obtain SYSTEM in seconds with no CVE needed.
Checks.Details: Privilege escalation risk factors: Print Spooler service is running (PrintNightmare surface open); SeImpersonatePrivilege available (Potato-family attacks feasible); Spooler driver store path is writable by current user.
Checks.Remediation: 1) Disable Print Spooler on non-print-servers: Stop-Service Spooler; Set-Service Spooler -StartupType Disabled. 2) Apply MS-MSHTML/CVE-2021-34527 patch. 3) Set PointAndPrint NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall=0. 4) Remove SeImpersonatePrivilege from non-service accounts via Group Policy (User Rights Assignment).

Checks.Name: Access Token Manipulation â€” Token Theft Prerequisite Audit
Checks.ThreatImpact: Token stealing allows an attacker with local admin access to silently impersonate any logged-in user, including Domain Admins. Mimikatz's sekurlsa::pth and the Windows built-in CreateProcessWithTokenW function require no additional exploit â€” just the right privileges.
Checks.Details: Token manipulation risk factors: SeDebugPrivilege held â€” can open any process; LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) not enabled; Credential Guard / VBS not enabled; lsaIso.exe not running (Credential Guard inactive). High-privilege token sources visible: lsass, winlogon, services.
Checks.Remediation: 1) Enable RunAsPPL: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa â†’ RunAsPPL=1. 2) Enable Credential Guard via UEFI Group Policy (Device Guard â†’ Turn On Virtualization Based Security). 3) Remove SeDebugPrivilege from non-debugger accounts. 4) Deploy Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to detect process injection and token duplication.

Checks.Name: UAC Bypass â€” CMSTPLUA / fodhelper Registry Hijack Detection
Checks.ThreatImpact: Over 60 documented UAC bypass techniques exist. The fodhelper and CMSTPLUA bypasses are built into popular red-team tools (Empire, Metasploit, Cobalt Strike) as one-click privilege escalation. A bypassed UAC means every subsequent command runs as a high-integrity Administrator with no prompt.
Checks.Details: UAC level 5 with secure desktop. No bypass artifacts detected.
Checks.Remediation: UAC is correctly configured. Continue monitoring for new bypass techniques.

Checks.Name: Lateral Token Theft â€” Stealing explorer.exe token
Checks.ThreatImpact: Token theft allows attackers (like Meterpreter or Cobalt Strike) to silently impersonate logged-on users, access mapped drives, and interact with the desktop without needing their plaintext passwords.
Checks.Details: Successfully duplicated the access token from explorer (PID: 4688) and spawned a new process impersonating its context. The host allowed lateral token theft.
Checks.Remediation: Ensure User Account Control (UAC) is strictly enforced to isolate tokens. Monitor for unexpected 'DuplicateTokenEx' and 'CreateProcessWithTokenW' invocations targeting shell processes.

Checks.Name: Vertical Privilege Escalation â€” Stealing svchost SYSTEM token
Checks.ThreatImpact: Stealing a SYSTEM token gives the attacker absolute control over the machine. They can disable security products, dump local credentials (LSASS), and establish deep stealth persistence.
Checks.Details: Access Denied when attempting to steal a SYSTEM token. Vertical privilege boundaries are properly intact.
Checks.Remediation: Maintain strict privilege isolation. Ensure LSA Protection is enabled.

Checks.Name: Protocol Steganography â€” Embedding data in benign HTTP Headers
Checks.ThreatImpact: Many web-proxies decrypt TLS but only perform signature matching on the URL or body. Hiding C2 data inside HTTP headers bypasses these checks cleanly.
Checks.Details: Successfully reached the internet with a standard HTTP GET request containing attacker payloads embedded in the Cookie, ETag, and Custom headers. Network filters and DPI did not sanitize or block anomalous long-string headers.
Checks.Remediation: Enforce strict HTTP protocol validation on the web proxy. Strip unrecognized X-Headers and enforce length/entropy limits on standard headers like Cookie and User-Agent.

Checks.Name: File Steganography â€” Appending data to valid Image uploads
Checks.ThreatImpact: Attackers often exfiltrate data by hiding it inside benign file types (e.g., appended to JPG or embedded in EXIF tags). Security gateways frequently ignore media files to save processing power.
Checks.Details: Successfully egressed an HTTP POST containing an image carrying appended plaintext strings. The firewall/DLP permitted the file structure anomaly without inspecting trailing binary data.
Checks.Remediation: Deploy Data Loss Prevention (DLP) or file-type anomaly inspection on egress gateways to evaluate file structure integrity, rather than just relying on MIME types or extensions.
